title: After Trump’s midterm defeat, Russia and China will encounter a cooler US
gist: Chatham House argues the 2026 midterms, which gave Democrats control of both the House and Senate, will impose a small but important constraint on Trump's foreign policy. Congress is expected to challenge any sustained US force deployment in the Gulf and reassert its authority over tariffs, while staying wary of Russia and China. Allies may become more assertive, and rivals will probe how far the US can hold its positions for more than a few years.

themes.theme: Iran war, Hormuz and affordability backlash

insights.claim: US voters ranked cost of living ('affordability') as their top concern in the 2026 midterms, while gasoline prices hit a high as they voted. The article attributes those rising costs largely to the continuing conflict around the Strait of Hormuz, which Trump started alongside Israel and has failed to end.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Ties oil and gasoline prices directly to US electoral outcomes; a Hormuz de-escalation would be the main policy lever for the affordability problem.
insights.quote: Rising costs are largely a result of the continued conflict in and around the Strait of Hormuz, which Americans know Trump initiated alongside Israel and has failed to end.
insights.locator: The most immediate change is likely

insights.claim: A Democratic-controlled Congress after the 2026 midterms is likely to challenge any sustained deployment of US forces in the Gulf, making the Iran conflict the most immediate area of foreign-policy change.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Congressional pressure against a long Gulf deployment lowers the odds of a drawn-out war premium in oil; watch for war-powers votes.
insights.quote: Congress is now likely to challenge any sustained deployment of forces in the Gulf.
insights.locator: Even with the Democrats in control

insights.claim: Trump might 'lash out' with more strikes on Iran after his midterm defeat to try to win concessions from Tehran, but the article sees no reason to think a military solution would work any better than before.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Short-term escalation risk and oil price spikes remain possible, but the author expects them to fail as a strategy, which points to eventual pressure for a negotiated end.
insights.quote: But there is no reason to believe that a military solution will fare any better than before.

insights.claim: The Republican Party has been among the biggest losers from the Iran war, so GOP candidates in the 2028 presidential race, which began once the midterm results were clear, are likely to be strongly against continuing the conflict. US pressure for a resolution would rise even if Israel's caretaker prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, pushed for a new assault.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Support for the war inside Trump's own party is fading, which makes a lasting US commitment to a Gulf conflict less likely, even if Israel pushes for one.
insights.quote: And GOP candidates are likely to be vehemently against continuing the conflict.
insights.locator: The Republican party has been among

themes.theme: Ukraine and Russia under the new Congress

insights.claim: The Democratic-controlled Congress will probably not send more arms or money to Ukraine, because both parties share a rare consensus that Europe should pay for its own defence, including support for Ukraine. Lawmakers feel Trump has won that argument and do not want to undo the victory.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Europe will keep carrying the cost of Ukraine and of its own rearmament whoever controls Congress, which supports long-term European defence spending.
insights.quote: There is deep, rare consensus among both Democrats and Republicans that Europe should now pay its way on its own defence – and that supporting Ukraine is part of that.

insights.claim: The new Congress does not share Trump's apparent warmth toward Vladimir Putin. Traditional hostility or wariness toward Moscow prevails and will constrain any business deals that Trump, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff offer the Kremlin in exchange for peace.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Peace deals built on US-Russia business ties, such as sanctions relief, face formal opposition in Congress, so expect any Russian normalisation to be slower and partial.
insights.quote: But they will be constrained by a tougher mood and even formal opposition in Congress.

insights.claim: As the midterm results became clear, Putin's spokesperson said he hoped peace-making efforts would continue. The article reads this as a sign the Kremlin fears the tougher congressional mood will close its channel to Trump.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Moscow has an incentive to lock in concessions quickly, before congressional constraints harden.
insights.quote: No wonder that Putin’s spokesperson said, as the results became clear, that he hoped peace-making efforts would continue.

insights.claim: One of the biggest disruptions Trump could cause in his remaining two years would be a deal with Beijing that explicitly acknowledged Taiwan as China's sovereign territory.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A tail risk for Taiwan-exposed assets, including semiconductors and regional security, that the author thinks Congress would push back against.

insights.claim: Trump recently paused a $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan to avoid aggravating trade relations with China, and Beijing could read the decision as support for its position on Taiwan.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Shows that trade ties with China now outrank Taiwan security commitments under Trump, a signal for defence contractors and for pricing Taiwan Strait risk.
insights.quote: Trump’s recent decision to pause a $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan, to avoid aggravating trade relations with China, could be interpreted by Beijing as support for its views.

insights.claim: Congress has been much warier of China than Trump across party lines, and some US tech companies now appear to be leaning toward that warier stance too.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Bipartisan and corporate hawkishness on China points to continued pressure on export controls and decoupling, whatever Trump does on trade.
insights.quote: It now seems that some tech companies are leaning that way too
insights.locator: Congress has, again across the political divide

themes.theme: Tariffs: revenue versus inflation and disruption

insights.claim: Trump's tariffs will stay for now, but Congress will reassert its authority over trade and has been challenging, through the Supreme Court, the president's right to impose tariffs without its consent.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Removing the tariffs requires legal or legislative action rather than a quick reversal; watch the Supreme Court route as the catalyst.
insights.quote: For the moment they will stay, although Congress has been challenging the president’s right to impose them without its consent, through the Supreme Court.
insights.locator: The fate of Trump’s tariffs is unclear.

insights.claim: Politicians across parties like tariffs for the revenue they raise, but the disruption to integrated supply chains (US car manufacturing was until last year interwoven with Canada's) and the inflation impact may lead affordability-focused politicians to look again at repealing them.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Pressure over affordability raises the odds that tariffs are eventually rolled back, which would help autos and other sectors with cross-border North American supply chains.
insights.quote: Politicians of all stripes find tariffs attractive for the revenue they bring.
insights.locator: Politicians of all stripes find tariffs

insights.claim: Economists hotly debate how much tariffs drive inflation, because inflation did not rise as much as expected when Trump's tariffs were first imposed.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The weak link between tariffs and inflation so far cuts against the affordability case for repeal, so a rollback is not a given.
insights.quote: That last point is hotly debated among economists given that inflation did not rise as much as expected when the tariffs were first imposed.
insights.locator: Politicians of all stripes find tariffs

themes.theme: How allies and rivals read a constrained US

insights.claim: The midterm results partly answer whether Americans really wanted Trump's actions and whether US democracy can still deliver peaceful changes of power, and some observers abroad will find that reassuring.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Less perceived risk to US institutions could ease the political-risk premium foreign investors place on US assets.
insights.quote: And is US democracy robust and capable of securing peaceful changes of power?

insights.claim: US allies in Europe, Japan and South Korea may become more confident in asserting their interests and values after the midterms, while remaining nervous about losing US support. Trump's sudden apparent removal of arms support to Israel just before the election shows how whimsical that support can be.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Allies are likely to hedge, asserting themselves more while building their own capabilities, which supports defence spending in Europe and Northeast Asia.
insights.quote: Trump’s sudden apparent removal of arms support to Israel in the days before the election shows how whimsical that can be.
insights.locator: For US allies in Europe, Japan

insights.claim: Russia and China will brace for cooler relations with the US, but will also probe for weakness by exploiting the repeated policy changes built into the US democratic system and the US's inability to hold its key positions consistently for more than a few years.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Rivals may adopt a 'wait out the cycle' strategy, which keeps geopolitical risk premia elevated around each US election.
insights.quote: But they will also explore the implications of the US being unable to hold consistently to its key positions for more than a few years.
insights.locator: For the US’s enemies and rivals

insights.claim: Given Trump's personality and desire for attention, impetuous and dramatic action on Iran or Taiwan cannot be ruled out. But he has lost his aura of being a winner, and politicians eyeing 2028 will distance themselves from him and try to constrain moves that could hurt their chances.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Lame-duck Trump is weaker politically but still unpredictable; keep tail-risk hedges on Iran and Taiwan even as his overall policy reach shrinks.
insights.quote: But he has lost any aura of being a winner that he retained.
